# Brief introduction

Acute Myloid Leukemia (AML) is a heterogeneous disease where different
cell types contribute in disparate ways towards cancer initiation and
progression. Therefore, to understand the biology of the disease, one
needs to study it at the most microscopic level possible. In light of
this and owing to my interest in cancer systems biology, I have chosen a
case-control single cell RNAseq (scRNAseq) dataset of AML
[@galen_single-cell_2019].

The dataset contains bone marrow cells, from 5 healthy donors and 16 AML
patients. Hence our control condition represents healthy hematopoeisis
(healthy blood formation), and our test condition is that of malignant
hematopoeisis (i.e. blood formation in AML). Given the scope of this
assignment, I have decided to include the following in my dataset: all
healthy cells and only a single AML patient's cells.

More detail on background, data inspection, and differential gene
expression analysis can be found in report 1 below.

## Thresholded over-representation analysis

### Creating a thresholded list from the DGE analysis

```{r}
# reading the gene list
degList <- as.data.frame(read_csv("degList.csv"))
row.names(degList) <- degList[["gene"]]

# thresholding the gene list based on adjusted pvalue
thresholdList <- degList[degList[["p_val_adj"]] < 0.05, ]

# up and down regulated gene sets
upReg <- thresholdList[thresholdList[["avg_log2FC"]] > 0, ]
downReg <- thresholdList[thresholdList[["avg_log2FC"]] < 0, ]

# show top 10 of each
```

### running g:profiler [@kolberg_gprofilerinteroperable_2023]

```{r}
querySet <- thresholdList$gene
organism <- "hsapiens"
gprofilerResults <- gost(
  query = querySet,
  significant = FALSE,
  ordered_query = FALSE,
  exclude_iea = TRUE,
  correction_method = "fdr",
  organism = organism,
  source = c("REAC", "WP", "GO:BP")
)
# get the gprofiler results table
gostplot(gprofilerResults, capped = TRUE, interactive = TRUE)
```

```{r, results='asis'}
enrichment_results <- gprofilerResults$result
cols <- c("source", "term_name", "p_value")
kable(enrichment_results[1:10, cols], caption = "Top 10 over represented genesets considering both up and down regulated genes")
```

### Question and answers

1.  Which method did you choose and why?<br> For creating a thresholded
    list, I used the cuttoff: adjusted p=value \< 0.05. Then used the
    genes in the thresholded list as the query list input to gprofiler.
    I use Benjamini-Hochberg FDR as the significance threshold to
    identify over represented gene sets.

2.  What annotation data did you use and why? What version of the
    annotation are you using?<br>

-   For the source of annotaion gene-sets, I am using the follwong
    databases: GO biological process (<GO:BP>), WikiPathways (WP), and
    Reactome (Reac).

```{r}
versionInfo <- get_version_info(organism = "hsapiens")$sources
cat("Version for GO biological process (GO:BP): ", versionInfo$`GO:BP`$version, "\n")
cat("Version for WikiPathways (WP): ", versionInfo$WP$version, "\n")
cat("Version for Reactome (Reac): ", versionInfo$REAC$version, "\n")
```

3.  How many genesets were returned with what thresholds?<br> The
    threshold chosen for a geneset to be significantly enriched is
    p-value \> 0.05. Below are the value counts of significantly vs
    insignificantly enriched genesets.

```{r, results='asis'}
kable(enrichment_results |> count(significant), caption = "Value counts for significant vs insignificant genesets as a result of gprofiler analysis")
```

4.  Run the analysis using the up-regulated set of genes, and the
    down-regulated set of genes separately. How do these results compare
    to using the whole list (i.e all differentially expressed genes
    together vs. the up-regulated and down regulated differentially
    expressed genes separately)?<br> The following is the comparison of
    over representation analysis when performed with only up or
    downregulated list of genes:

```{r}
querySetUp <- upReg$gene
querySetDown <- downReg$gene


gprofilerResultsForUp <- gost(
  query = querySetUp,
  significant = FALSE,
  ordered_query = FALSE,
  exclude_iea = TRUE,
  correction_method = "fdr",
  organism = organism,
  source = c("REAC", "WP", "GO:BP")
)

gprofilerResultsForDown <- gost(
  query = querySetDown,
  significant = FALSE,
  ordered_query = FALSE,
  exclude_iea = TRUE,
  correction_method = "fdr",
  organism = organism,
  source = c("REAC", "WP", "GO:BP")
)

enrichmentResultsForUp <- gprofilerResultsForUp$result
enrichmentResultsForDown <- gprofilerResultsForDown$result


cat("Number of genesets significantly enriched when using up + down regulated DEGs:", count(enrichment_results, significant) |> filter(significant == TRUE) |> pull(n), "\n")
cat("Number of genesets significantly enriched when using only up regulated DEGs:", count(enrichmentResultsForUp, significant) |> filter(significant == TRUE) |> pull(n), "\n")
cat("Number of genesets significantly enriched when using only down regulated DEGs:", count(enrichmentResultsForDown, significant) |> filter(significant == TRUE) |> pull(n), "\n")
```

The following dataframe represents name of top 10 over-represented
gene-sets for all the 3 cases:

```{r, results='asis'}
kable(as.data.frame(list(
  "up plus down" = enrichment_results$term_name[1:10],
  "up" = enrichmentResultsForUp$term_name[1:10],
  "down" = enrichmentResultsForDown$term_name[1:10]
)), caption = "Naive comparisson of the results with 3 different genesets permutations")
```

NOTE: This is not a robust analysis, one could use set distance measures
like jaccard similarity or plot a simple pie chart to see overlapping
genesets when comparing the 3 variants of over representation analysis.
Performing thereof analysis is out of the scope for this assignment.

### Interpretation

Van Galen et al., the authors of the paper accompanying the data, did
not particularly analyzed the transcriptional profiles of all individual
cell types. In this report I analyze transcriptional differences in
healthy vs malignant promonocyte cells.

1.  Do the over-representation results support conclusions or mechanism
    discussed in the original paper?

One of the major themes that come out of my analysis is enrichment of
genesets related to ribosomal biogenesis and translation. Upon reviewing
existing literature, I found out that dysregulated ribosomal biogenesis
is a widely recognized driver of tumorigenesis [@gitareja_ribosome_2025].

2.  Can you find evidence, i.e. publications, to support some of the
    results that you see. How does this evidence support your results.

This research by Chen et al elucidates the role of dysregulated
ribosomal biogenesis specifically in AML [@chen_elucidating_2025]. Genesets related to translation
are upregulated as the rapid and continuous proliferation of cancer
cells requires continuous protein synthesis and increased ribosome
content.

## Non-thresholded Gene set Enrichment Analysis [@subramanian_gene_2005]

```{r, parameter_setup}
# Setting up parameters
gseaJar <- "/home/rstudio/GSEA_4.4.0/gsea-cli.sh"
workingDir <- getwd()

if (!dir.exists("./gsea_results")) {
  dir.create("./gsea_results")
}
outputDir <- paste(getwd(), "gsea_results", sep = "/")

# we set up destGmtFile to be "" so it fetches the latest one from the bader lab website
destGmtFile <- ""
runGSEA <- TRUE
analysisName <- "promono_healthy_vs_leukemia_expression"
rankFile <- "promono_healthy_vs_leukemia_expression.rnk"
```

### Creating a non thresholded list from the DGE analysis

The code below was used to generate the ranks file which is required as
an input to GSEA.

```{r}
rankedList <- degList
rankedList[, "rank"] <- log10(rankedList$p_val) * sign(rankedList$avg_log2FC)
rankedList <- arrange(rankedList, desc(rank))
if (!file.exists(rankFile)) {
  write.table(rankedList[c("gene", "rank")], file = rankFile, quote = FALSE, sep = "\t", row.names = FALSE)
}
```

Initially, I tried running GSEA using R but couldn't do it; below is my
code. Therefore, GSEA analysis was performed using the application GUI.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
if (runGSEA) {
  command <- paste("", gseaJar,
    "GSEAPreRanked -gmx", destGmtFile,
    "-rnk", file.path(workingDir, rankFile),
    "-collapse false -nperm 1000 -scoring_scheme weighted",
    "-rpt_label ", analysisName,
    "  -plot_top_x 20 -rnd_seed 12345  -set_max 200",
    " -set_min 15 -zip_report false ",
    " -out", outputDir,
    " > ./gsea_results/gsea_output.txt",
    sep = " "
  )
  system(command)
}
```

### Question and answers

1.  What method did you use? What genesets did you use? Make sure to
    specify versions and cite your methods.

I performed GSEA using the GUI of the application
[@subramanian_gene_2005]. I used the C5 geneset provided in the MsigDB.
It comprises of gene sets that contain genes annotated by the same
ontology term. C5 collection is divided into two subcollections, the
first derived from the Gene Ontology resource (GO) which contains BP,
CC, and MF components and a second derived from the Human Phenotype
Ontology (HPO). I used both the subcollections. I used the 2026 version
specified by the follwing gmt file: `c5.all.v2026.1.Hs.symbols.gmt`.

2.  Summarize your enrichment results.

GSEA report contains two “Enrichment in Phenotype” sections. The first
section shows results for gene sets that have a positive enrichment
score (gene sets that show enrichment at the top of the ranked list) and
the second section shows results for gene sets that have a negative
enrichment score (gene sets that show enrichment at the bottom of the
ranked list). Below are the names corresponding to top 10 enriched
genesets for both the cases.

```{r}
upRegGeneSets <- read.delim("gsea_report_for_na_pos_1773179948718.tsv", sep = "\t")
downRegGeneSets <- read.delim("gsea_report_for_na_neg_1773179948718.tsv", sep = "\t")
cols <- c("NAME", "FDR.q.val", "SIZE")

kable(upRegGeneSets[1:10, cols], caption = "Top 10 genesets with positive enrichment scores")
```

```{r}
kable(downRegGeneSets[1:10, cols], caption = "Top 10 genesets with negative enrichment scores")
```

## Visualizing Gene set Enrichment Analysis in Cytoscape

We will use the results from non-thresholded gene set enrichment
analysis to visualize them in Cytoscape [@shannon_cytoscape_2003].

### Question and answers

1.  Create an enrichment map - how many nodes and how many edges in the
    resulting map? What thresholds were used to create this map? Make
    sure to record all thresholds. Include a screenshot of your network
    prior to manual layout.

To create the enrichment map, first I thoroughly read the following
enrichment map documentation
<https://enrichmentmap.readthedocs.io/en/latest/index.html>. As
described in the "Tips on parameter choice section", I decided to use
very permissive thresholds of p-value \< 0.05, FDR \< 0.25, and a
moderately conservative overlap threshold of 0.5
[@merico_enrichment_2010.

## Interpretation and detailed view of results

Here I will relate my results back to the initial data and question.

1.  Do the enrichment results support conclusions or mechanism discussed
    in the original paper? How do these results differ from the results
    you got from Assignment #2 thresholded methods

Clearly, enrichment of genesets related to ribosome function and
cytoplasmic translation appears to be a major theme from both
thresholded and non-thresholded analysis. This is in line with overall
context of this data. Since we are comparing malignant cells to healthy
cells, its indeed not surprising that genesets related to translation
are upregulated as the rapid and continuous proliferation of cancer
cells requires continuous protein synthesis and increased ribosome
content [@robichaud_translational_2019].

2.  Can you find evidence, i.e. publications, to support some of the
    results that you see. How does this evidence support your result?

We see upregulation of translation related genes like elongation
factors. This finding is supported by Robivhaud et al. in a review about
translational control in cancer, whereby they
describe—mechanistically—the implications of this finding in the context
of cancer [@robichaud_translational_2019].
